---
id: "smk-16"
title: "The Nile"
---

The Nile is a river in north-eastern Africa that has traditionally been regarded as the longest river in the world, at about 6,650 kilometres. It has two main branches: the White Nile, which begins in the Great Lakes region near Lake Victoria, and the Blue Nile, which rises at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian highlands and contributes most of the water and silt. The two branches meet at Khartoum in Sudan, and the river then flows north through the desert to Egypt, ending in a fan-shaped delta on the Mediterranean Sea. The annual flood of the Nile deposited fertile soil along its banks and made possible the agriculture on which ancient Egyptian civilisation depended. The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, now regulates the flow and generates electricity, while also holding back the silt. Eleven countries share the basin, and the allocation of Nile water remains a matter of negotiation among them.
